newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's Alarcon walks thin line seeking consensus.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's Alarcon walks thin line seeking consensus.

text.p: New Ecuadorean President Fabian Alarcon sought on Friday to find a middle ground that would satisfy the populist groups that brought him to power while addressing the need for economic reform.

Alarcon, sworn in on Tuesday by Congress in the midst of a political crisis, had a tight agenda of meetings with leaders of groups and political parties which backed last week's removal of President Abdala Bucaram.
"The president is searching for consensus between the different popular groups," a presidential spokesman told Reuters.
Immediately after taking office, Alarcon ditched several economic measures which sparked widespread protests and a 48-hour general strike against Bucaram.

The eccentric former president, whose austerity reforms were meant to pave the way for a new currency plan designed by former Argentine Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo, was dismissed by Congress last week on grounds of "mental incompetence."
Alarcon has said he will not be able to make too many concessions to his populist backers in view of Ecuador's budget shortfall.
"The situation in which we have received the country ... is really catastrophic," Alarcon told reporters on Thursday. "We've been on the verge of collapse ... economically and socially."
Alarcon said within the next two or three months he would pass measures to mend the economy and plug a fiscal hole estimated this year at between five and seven percent of GDP.
But uncertainty over the direction of his government spread with the first Cabinet announcements on Thursday.

Economist Carlos Davalos Rodas, appointed finance minister, has participated in leftist governments and was economic adviser to former president Rodrigo Borja, who suspended foreign debt interest payments.
Davalos made few public statements on Thursday but hinted the currency plan, due to start in June, would be scrapped.
On Friday Alarcon named Raul Baca as energy minister, bowing to trade union demands. Baca has been an outspoken critic of privatisation plans in the energy sector.

The unions and indigenous groups are pressuring Alarcon and have threatened to resume protests if he introduces the same free market policies as Bucaram, while analysts have voiced fears that his political coalition is made up of partners backing contradictory economic platforms -- a recipe for future instability.
